question: Under the Standardised Approach, what risk weight applies to both fund-based and non-fund based claims on the central government?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.2.1
source_excerpt: Both fund based and non-fund based claims on the central government will attract a zero risk weight. Central Government guaranteed claims will attract a zero risk weight.

question: What risk weight do claims guaranteed by a State Government attract under the Standardised Approach?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.2.2
source_excerpt: The Direct loan / credit / overdraft exposure, if any, of banks to the State Governments and the investment in State Government securities will attract zero risk weight. State Government guaranteed claims will attract 20 per cent risk weight.

question: As per Table 1 of the circular, what risk weight applies to claims on a foreign sovereign rated BBB by S&P/Fitch?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.3, Table 1
source_excerpt: S&P*/Fitch ratings AAA to AA A BBB BB to B Below B Unrated Moody’s ratings Aaa to Aa A Baa Ba to B Below B Unrated Risk weight (%) 0 20 50 100 150 100

question: How does the circular prescribe that claims on domestic public sector entities be risk weighted?
options: In a manner similar to the claims on sovereigns and central governments
In a manner similar to claims on corporates
With a uniform risk weight of 20 per cent
In a manner similar to the claims on banks
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.4.1
source_excerpt: Claims on domestic public sector entities will be risk weighted in a manner similar to claims on Corporates.

topic: risk weights - MDBs, BIS and IMF
question: What risk weight do claims on the BIS, the IMF and the eligible Multilateral Development Banks evaluated by the BCBS attract?
options: A uniform zero per cent risk weight
A uniform twenty per cent risk weight
A uniform fifty per cent risk weight
Risk weights as per the ratings assigned to them
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.5
source_excerpt: Claims on the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the following eligible Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) evaluated by the BCBS will be treated similar to claims on scheduled banks meeting the minimum capital adequacy requirements and assigned a uniform twenty per cent risk weight

question: Claims on a bank denominated in 'domestic' foreign currency and met out of resources in the same currency raised in that jurisdiction attract which risk weight when the bank complies with the minimum CRAR prescribed by its regulator?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.6.3
source_excerpt: However, the claims on a bank which are denominated in 'domestic 35' foreign currency met out of the resources in the same currency raised in that jurisdiction will be risk weighted at 20 per cent provided the bank complies with the minimum CRAR prescribed by the concerned bank regulator(s).

question: Under Table 5 Part A, what risk weight applies to a long-term claim on a corporate assigned an AA rating by a domestic rating agency?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.8, Table 5
source_excerpt: Domestic rating agencies AAA AA A BBB BB & below Unrated Risk weight (%) 20 30 50 100 150 100

question: What risk weight is assigned to claims included in a regulatory retail portfolio, except as provided for non-performing assets?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.9.1
source_excerpt: Claims (including both fund-based and non-fund based) that meet all the four criteria listed below in paragraph 5.9.3 may be considered as retail claims for regulatory capital purposes and included in a regulatory retail portfolio. Claims included in this portfolio shall be assigned a risk - weight of 75 per cent, except as provided in paragraph 5.12 below for non-performing assets.

question: For claims secured by residential property that fall outside the categories in Table 7, what risk weight does the circular prescribe?
options: A uniform risk weight of 35 per cent irrespective of the purpose of finance
The higher of the risk weight applicable to the counterparty or to the purpose for which the bank has extended finance
The lower of the counterparty risk weight and 75 per cent
A risk weight of 100 per cent irrespective of the counterparty
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.10.2
source_excerpt: All other claims secured by residential property would attract the higher of the risk weight applicable to the counterparty or to the purpose for which the bank has extended finance.

question: What risk weight do claims classified as commercial real estate exposure attract?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.11
source_excerpt: Commercial Real Estate exposure is defined as per the guidelines issued vide circular DBOD.No.BP.BC.42/08.12.015/2009-10 dated September 9, 2009. 5.11.2 Claims mentioned above will attract a risk weight of 100 per cent.

question: Under the risk-weighting framework for non-performing assets, what risk weight applies to the unsecured portion of an NPA when specific provisions are at least 50 per cent of the outstanding amount?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.12.1
source_excerpt: (iii) 50 per cent risk weight when specific provisions are at least 50 per cent of the outstanding amount of the NPA

question: When defining the secured portion of an NPA for capital adequacy purposes, which collateral is recognised?
options: Collateral recognised for credit risk mitigation purposes under paragraph 7.3.5
Land and building valued by an expert valuer with a valuation not more than three years old
Plant and machinery in good working condition at a value not higher than the depreciated value
Current assets of the borrower irrespective of their realisable value
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.12.3
source_excerpt: For the purpose of defining the secured portion of the NPA, eligible collateral will be the same as recognised for credit risk mitigation purposes (paragraph 7.3.5).

question: What risk weight does the circular prescribe for consumer credit exposure, including personal loans, that excludes housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans and loans secured by gold and gold jewellery?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.13.3
source_excerpt: Consumer credit exposure (outstanding as well as new), including personal loans, but excluding housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans and loans secured by gold and gold jewellery, will attract a risk weight of 125 per cent47.

question: What credit conversion factor does Table 8 assign to direct credit substitutes such as general guarantees of indebtedness and acceptances?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.15.2, Table 8
source_excerpt: 1. Direct credit substitutes e.g., general guarantees of indebtedness (including standby L/Cs serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities for securitisation transactions), and acceptances (including endorsements with the character of acceptance). question: An irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 15 months to issue a six-month documentary letter of credit attracts which credit conversion factor?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.15.2
source_excerpt: Irrevocable commitments to provide off-balance sheet facilities should be assigned the lower of the two applicable credit conversion factors. For example, an irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 15 months (50 per cent - CCF) to issue a six month documentary letter of credit (20 per cent - CCF) would attract the lower of the CCF i.e., the CCF applicable to the documentary letter of credit viz. 20 per cent.

question: Which of the following is eligible financial collateral under the comprehensive approach?
options: Re-securitisations, irrespective of any credit ratings
Gold, including both bullion and jewellery
Land and building that are valued by an expert valuer
Units of mutual funds where no price for the units is publicly quoted daily
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.5
source_excerpt: Gold: Gold would include both bullion and jewellery. However, the value of the collateralised jewellery should be arrived at after notionally converting these to 99.99 purity.

question: Which international credit rating agencies may banks use for risk weighting their claims where specified?
options: Fitch, SEBI and CRISIL Ratings Limited
Moody's, ICRA Limited and CARE Ratings Limited
Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, Brickwork Ratings India Private Limited and INFOMERICS Valuation and Rating Ltd.
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.1.3
source_excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has decided that banks may use the ratings of the following international credit rating agencies (arranged in alphabetical order) for the purposes of risk weighting their claims for capital adequacy purposes where specified: a. Fitch; b. Moody's; and c. Standard & Poor’s

question: Which of the following lists only domestic credit rating agencies whose ratings banks may use for risk weighting their claims?
options: CRISIL Ratings Limited, ICRA Limited and the Securities and Exchange Board of India
Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, CARE Ratings Limited and Moody's

Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, Brickwork Ratings India Private Limited, CARE Ratings Limited, CRISIL Ratings Limited, ICRA Limited, India Ratings and Research Private Limited and INFOMERICS Valuation and Rating Ltd.

question: Under the mapping of long-term ratings of the chosen domestic rating agencies, what risk weight is assigned to a rating of A+ or A-?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.4.2
source_excerpt: For example, A+ or A - would be considered to be in the A rating category and assigned 50 per cent risk weight.

question: If a short-term rated facility to a counterparty attracts a 50 per cent risk weight, what is the lowest risk weight that unrated short-term claims to the same counterparty may attract?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.5.2
source_excerpt: If a short-term rated facility to counterparty attracts a 20 per cent or a 50 per cent risk-weight, unrated short-term claims to the same counter- party cannot attract a risk weight lower than 30 per cent or 100 per cent respectively.

question: Which of the following is a general principle governing the use of credit risk mitigation techniques?
options: The effects of credit risk mitigation may be double counted where an issue-specific rating is used
A transaction using credit risk mitigation techniques should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used
No transaction in which credit risk mitigation techniques are used should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used
Principal-only ratings are allowed within the credit risk mitigation framework
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.1.2
source_excerpt: No transaction in which Credit Risk Mitigation (CRM) techniques are used should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used.

question: What minimum legal documentation standard must be satisfied for a bank to obtain capital relief for credit risk mitigation?
options: Documentation must be notarised in each district where the bank has branches
All documentation used in collateralised transactions and guarantees must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions
Documentation need only be enforceable in the jurisdiction where the counterparty is incorporated
Legal review is optional where the collateral consists of cash
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.2
source_excerpt: All documentation used in collateralised transactions and guarantees must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions.

question: Which approach to collateralised transactions shall banks in India adopt for credit risk mitigation?
options: The simple approach, which substitutes the risk weighting of the collateral for the risk weighting of the counterparty for the collateralised portion
The standardised approach for market risk
The basic indicator approach for operational risk
The comprehensive approach, which allows fuller offset of collateral against exposures by effectively reducing the exposure amount by the value ascribed to the collateral
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.2
source_excerpt: Banks in India shall adopt the Comprehensive Approach, which allows fuller offset of collateral against exposures, by effectively reducing the exposure amount by the value ascribed to the collateral.

question: What standard supervisory haircut applies where the exposure and the collateral are denominated in different currencies?
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.7
source_excerpt: The standard supervisory haircut for currency risk where exposure and collateral are denominated in different currencies is eight per cent (also based on a 10-business day holding period and daily mark-to-market).

question: Under the substitution approach for guarantees, how does credit protection reduce the capital requirement?
options: The whole exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor irrespective of the amount covered
The risk weight of the counterparty is reduced by the guarantee coverage percentage
Capital charges are reduced even when the guarantor has a higher risk weight than the counterparty
The protected portion of the counterparty exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor, whereas the uncovered portion retains the risk weight of the underlying counterparty
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.5.2
source_excerpt: A range of guarantors are recognised and a substitution approach will be applied. Thus , only guarantees issued by entities with a lower risk weight than the counterparty will lead to reduced capital charges since the protected portion of the counterparty exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor, whereas the uncovered portion retains the risk weight of the underlying counterparty.
